translation:
Master Han of Changli said, "If there is none to go before, then though a thing be beautiful it will not be made manifest; if there is none to come after, then though it be flourishing it will not be transmitted." Truly these words are excellent. For a thousand years above and below, we rely on continuation. Otherwise, what the men of former times achieved through painstaking thought and accumulated care, the men of later times would only watch as it perished and was utterly extinguished. If one does not receive from the past to open the way for the future, how nearly would the whole world become blind! For this reason, the gentleman who embraces the remnants and guards the deficiencies pays special attention to the lost learning—and rightly so. When Sima Qian completed his writing, in his own preface he said, "Hide it in a famous mountain, and transmit it to the right person." Alas, how easily is that person obtained! Master Hu Zhijiao of Guichuan loves learning and admires antiquity, is broad in arts and many in abilities. Because he is broad in arts, he cherishes the arts as his very life; because he admires antiquity, he fears that antiquity will sink into oblivion. As for what he has learned and can do, I gaze upon its vastness but cannot fathom its shores. Now especially, in his collating and printing of the True Meaning of Enlightenment, he lifts a single ladle of it, wishing to measure it together with the world. The True Meaning of Enlightenment is what Guichuan named by combining the two schools of ophthalmology. One is the work of Master Deng Bowang of Qingjiang, who has the Complete Book of Ophthalmology of the One-Grass Pavilion, whose original text is damaged and incomplete. The other, by an unknown author, is the Secretly Transmitted Ophthalmology, which remains in the world between heaven and earth, possessing the skill of sweeping away clouds and the marvel of parting mist. In the Kangxi reign, Lord Nian Xiyao reprinted the Deng book and also engraved the Secretly Transmitted text for the first time. Now, though I search everywhere, I cannot obtain its edition. A pity, a pity—its learning is cut off! I am by nature unrestrained and wild, not content to remain beneath the window; I have long loved to travel and have made many acquaintances among scholars and officials. What I have seen in passing—the splendor of brocade, the abundance of treasures, the dazzling and bizarre things that astonish the eyes and ears of the vulgar—such things are everywhere. Yet I regard them as nothing, and my two eyes are as if blind. Now, I am not blind in the eyes, yet I am as if blind in the eyes; from this I know that those others are not blind in the eyes, but in truth are not only blind in the eyes but also blind in the heart. Alas, alas—who has caused the unlearned of the world to be thus blinded? In the spring of the gengchen year of the Guangxu reign, I came down from Longmian and entered Min. The one I found congenial at first sight was none other than Hu Guichuan. I arrived at his hall, where several famous paintings and calligraphies hung, the furnishings sparse, plain and close to antiquity. I bowed, sat, and conversed with him; his bearing was dignified and his words all had substance. When I withdrew I said to myself, "This man can open my blindness." Before long, I know not from where Guichuan took me, but he invited me to lodge in his house and had his young son receive the classics from me. The days and months passed, and the cold and heat have already changed twice to the present. When I first came to his house, I did not expect that in my mind and eyes I would despise those things and suddenly be dazzled by these. Why is it so? Ascend his hall—there are only books; enter his study—there are only books; rest in his chambers—there are only books. Jade cases pile up like mountains, ivory book labels accumulate in clusters. Compared to brocade and treasures, their dazzling and bizarre splendor is severalfold greater. This is the utmost of sights; nothing can be added to it. The longer I lodged in his house, the more I knew that Guichuan is deep in the classics, versed in history, weaving together the words of the hundred schools, and especially profound in the learning of Qi and Huang. And not only this. There is something even more remarkable: astrology; he points to chess, go, and geomancy; he seizes the dragon and tiger and the yang dwellings; he consults the hexagrams and divination; he hangs the tortoise mirror and practices the Six Ren, and is especially skilled in physiognomy. With his single eye, beauty and ugliness, good and evil, the deviant and the upright, fortune and misfortune all appear and cannot hide their forms. As for the divine peak, he brings the poverty and success, longevity and early death of the whole world into the palm of his hand. As for the art of war, he has tried it—he killed bandits at Hu and Xiang, but in a time of peace it had no use, and Guichuan kept it secret and never spoke of it. All these are indeed Guichuan's brocade, Guichuan's treasures, the dazzling and bizarre things stored within his breast and belly—how could they be only the learning of Qi and Huang? Qi and Huang is but one puddle in the vast ocean. For this reason, in what he now collates and prints, he is earnest and eager, taking delight only in continuing the lost learning of antiquity through me. Alas, the worthies Bowang and others, having been cut off, are now continued from this day forward. If it were not for Guichuan, who loves learning, admires antiquity, is broad in arts and many in abilities, by what would it be transmitted, and where would that person be obtained? If this book had fallen only into the hands of others, those who carelessly do not treasure it would cast it upon the shelves; if not eaten by bookworms and gnawed by rats, it would leak from above and be dampened below, rotting beyond repair, cast into an old basket and thrown into water and fire—who would pass by and ask about it? Those who know it to be a treasure would again hide it deeply and keep it secret, alone holding it as a rarity, privately keeping its art, seeking profit in the world, treating the blind of the world in order to blind the eyes and ears of the world, making the crowd marvel at it as a unique and unprecedented skill—this only broadens its fame, but in the end it too comes to the same extinction. Then the two kinds of men who hide it in a famous mountain and transmit it to the right person—are they indeed that person? Now Guichuan, cherishing it to the utmost and fearing it deeply, cherishing that its art is about to be cut off and fearing that antiquity will sink into oblivion, raises it up and prints it to spread it widely through the world. It is transmitted. The worthies Bowang and others are not only the glory of that one time; if men of later ages are skilled in its art and good at using it, they will all take the True Meaning of Enlightenment as their ancestor. Holding the art to achieve fame, name and art will surely shine forth. Alas, Guichuan is but one man—above, he faces antiquity; below, he welcomes the future, being the one who comes after and the one who goes before. Truly he wishes to hold this to keep the world from blindness; how can the world fathom it? Alas, alas—I am by nature unrestrained and wild, and I wish to proclaim loudly to the world: the blind need not be blind, and those who are not blind should not bring themselves to blindness. One should preserve one's eyes as one preserves one's heart.

<ins>Preface by Zhang Shouliu, styled Zhuowo, of Wantong, in the first ten days of the first month of the renwu year of the Guangxu reign</ins>
translator_notes: 昌黎韓子 (Master Han of Changli) refers to Han Yu.
史遷 (Shi Qian) refers to Sima Qian.
光怪陸離 (guangguai luli) means dazzling and bizarre.
六壬 (Six Ren) is a form of divination.
神峰 (divine peak) appears to refer to physiognomy.
